title: Unit Circle & Radians
description: Degree-radian conversion, arc length and sector area, exact values at special angles, ASTC signs, and reference and coterminal angles.

cards.title: What is one radian, and about how many degrees is it?
cards.body:
The central angle whose intercepted arc is exactly one radius long: about $57.3^\circ$.

The circumference is $2\pi r$, which is $2\pi$ radii, so a full turn is $2\pi$ radians.

So $360^\circ = 2\pi\text{ rad}$ and $1\text{ rad} = \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$. Use **radians** whenever you apply $s = r\theta$.

Key idea: an angle in radians is arc length measured in radii.
Watch out: one radian is not $1^\circ$; it is a bit under $60^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: radian definition arc length equals radius degrees

cards.title: Convert $210^\circ$ to radians (exact form).
cards.body:
$\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$

Multiply degrees by $\frac{\pi}{180}$: $210 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{7\pi}{6}$.

Why: $180^\circ = \pi$ rad, so the factor $\frac{\pi}{180}$ cancels the degree unit.

Tip: $30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}$, and $210^\circ = 7 \cdot 30^\circ$, so you can count in sixths.

cards.title: Convert $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ radians to degrees.
cards.body:
$300^\circ$

Multiply **radians** by $\frac{180}{\pi}$: $\frac{5\pi}{3} \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} = 5 \cdot 60 = 300$.

Tip: $\frac{\pi}{3} = 60^\circ$, so $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ is $5$ of those, or $300^\circ$.
Watch out: use $\frac{180}{\pi}$ to go to degrees and $\frac{\pi}{180}$ to go to radians; swapping them is the usual slip.

cards.title: Exact length of the arc cut off by a central angle of $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ on a circle of radius $6\,\text{cm}$?
cards.body:
$4\pi\,\text{cm} \approx 12.57\,\text{cm}$

Use $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in **radians**: $6 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} = 4\pi$ cm.

Why: radian measure is arc length divided by radius, so arc length is radius times angle.
Watch out: plugging in degrees ($120$) gives $720$, which is wrong; convert to radians first.
cards.searchQuery: arc length formula s = r theta radians

cards.title: Exact area of a sector with radius $4$ and central angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$?
cards.body:
$2\pi$ square units

Use $A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ with $\theta$ in **radians**: $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 16 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} = 2\pi$ square units.

Why: $\frac{\pi}{4}$ is $\frac{1}{8}$ of a full turn, and $\frac{1}{8}$ of the disk area $\pi r^2 = 16\pi$ is $2\pi$.
Watch out: do not forget the $\frac{1}{2}$ or square the angle.

cards.title: If the terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(x, y)$, what are $\cos\theta$, $\sin\theta$, and $\tan\theta$?
cards.body:
$\cos\theta = x$, $\sin\theta = y$, $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$ (when $x \ne 0$).

Every point on the unit circle is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, so cosine is the **$x$-coordinate** and sine is the **$y$-coordinate**.

Tangent is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$, defined only when $x \ne 0$.

Example: $\theta = \pi$ lands at $(-1, 0)$, so $\cos\pi = -1$, $\sin\pi = 0$ and $\tan\pi = 0$.
Mnemonic: cosine comes first alphabetically, like $x$ in the pair $(x, y)$.
cards.searchQuery: unit circle cosine sine tangent definition x y

cards.title: What pattern gives $\sin\theta$ at $\theta = 0, \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}$, and how do the cosines relate?
cards.body:
$\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{4}}{2}$, that is, $0, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 1$.

The sines at $0, \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}$ are the **square roots** of $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$, each divided by $2$.

Cosine runs the same list backward, from $\cos 0 = 1$ down to $\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$. So $\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$.

Tip: you only have to memorize one quadrant; the others follow by reference angles and signs.
cards.searchQuery: unit circle special angles sine pattern sqrt over 2

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan\frac{\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$\sqrt{3}$

$\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{\cos(\pi/3)} = \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = \sqrt{3}$.

Tangent is the slope of the terminal side, and the $60^\circ$ line is steeper than the $30^\circ$ line.

Watch out: do not swap it with $\tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$, which is the smaller value.

cards.title: For which angles $\theta$ is $\tan\theta$ undefined? Give the general form and the angles in $[0, 2\pi)$.
cards.body:
$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$ for any integer $k$; in $[0, 2\pi)$ that's $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

$\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ is undefined where $\cos\theta = 0$, that is, where $x = 0$ on the unit circle.

That happens at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$; in $[0, 2\pi)$ these are $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

Key idea: $\sec\theta$ is undefined at the **same angles**, since it also divides by cosine.
cards.searchQuery: tangent undefined angles pi/2 plus k pi

cards.title: Which trig functions are positive in each of the four quadrants?
cards.body:
QI: all six. QII: sine and cosecant. QIII: tangent and cotangent. QIV: cosine and secant.

The signs come from $x = \cos\theta$, $y = \sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$.

- **QI**: all six are positive
- **QII**: sine and cosecant
- **QIII**: tangent and cotangent
- **QIV**: cosine and secant

Mnemonic: ASTC, "All Students Take Calculus", counterclockwise from QI.
cards.searchQuery: ASTC unit circle quadrant signs trig functions

cards.title: Which angle in $[0, 2\pi)$ is coterminal with $-\frac{7\pi}{6}$? Answer in radians.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

Coterminal angles differ by multiples of $2\pi$. Add $2\pi = \frac{12\pi}{6}$: $-\frac{7\pi}{6} + \frac{12\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.

Example: for $\frac{17\pi}{4}$, subtract $4\pi$ to get $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
Tip: write $2\pi$ with the same denominator as the angle before adding or subtracting.
cards.searchQuery: coterminal angle in 0 to 2pi negative radians

cards.title: What is the reference angle of $\theta = \frac{7\pi}{5}$, in radians?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$

The **reference angle** is the acute angle between the terminal side and the $x$-axis. $\frac{7\pi}{5}$ lies between $\pi$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, in QIII, so subtract $\pi$: $\frac{7\pi}{5} - \pi = \frac{2\pi}{5}$.

- QII: $\pi - \theta$
- QIII: $\theta - \pi$
- QIV: $2\pi - \theta$

Tip: first place the angle by its decimal size, since $\frac{7\pi}{5}$ is $252^\circ$.

cards.title: At what exact point does the terminal side of $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ meet the unit circle?
cards.body:
$\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

$\frac{2\pi}{3}$ is in QII with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$. The point is $\left(-\cos\frac{\pi}{3}, \sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

Why: in QII the $x$-coordinate (cosine) is negative and the $y$-coordinate (sine) is positive.
Tip: take the reference-angle point from QI, then attach the quadrant's signs.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

$\frac{5\pi}{4} = \pi + \frac{\pi}{4}$ is in QIII with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, which is negative in QIII, so $\cos\frac{5\pi}{4} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

Watch out: the reference angle gives the **size** only; the quadrant gives the sign.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{1}{2}$

$\frac{7\pi}{6} = \pi + \frac{\pi}{6}$ is in QIII with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$.

Sine is the $y$-coordinate, which is negative in QIII, so $\sin\frac{7\pi}{6} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}$.

Watch out: do not use $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$; that is the cosine at the same reference angle.

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan\frac{11\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$, equivalently $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\frac{11\pi}{6} = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$ is in QIV with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$.

Tangent $= \frac{y}{x}$ is negative in QIV, so $\tan\frac{11\pi}{6} = -\tan\frac{\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.

Tip: $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ and $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ are the same number.

cards.title: What does it mean for an angle to be in standard position?
cards.body:
Its vertex is at the origin and its initial side lies along the positive $x$-axis.

The **terminal side** is where the rotation ends. Measuring every angle from the same ray is what lets unit-circle coordinates define the trig functions.

Key idea: two angles in standard position are equal exactly when they share the same terminal side and the same rotation.
cards.searchQuery: angle standard position initial side terminal side

cards.title: In standard position, does a positive angle rotate clockwise or counterclockwise from the initial side?
cards.body:
Counterclockwise.

Clockwise rotation gives a **negative** angle.

Example: $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ ends on the negative $y$-axis, the same terminal side as $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

Tip: this is the same convention as the polar angle in calculus.
cards.searchQuery: positive angle direction counterclockwise standard position

cards.title: What is a quadrantal angle? List the quadrantal angles in $[0, 2\pi)$.
cards.body:
An angle whose terminal side lies on a coordinate axis. In $[0, 2\pi)$: $0$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

In general the quadrantal angles are $\frac{k\pi}{2}$ for integers $k$. They lie in **no quadrant**, and their unit-circle points are $(\pm 1, 0)$ and $(0, \pm 1)$.

Watch out: at these angles one of $x$ or $y$ is $0$, so some functions are undefined (for example $\tan\frac{\pi}{2}$).
cards.searchQuery: quadrantal angle definition terminal side on axis

cards.title: Convert $135^\circ$ to radians (exact form).
cards.body:
$\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

$135 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{135\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4}$.

Tip: $135^\circ = 3 \cdot 45^\circ$, and $45^\circ = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

cards.title: Convert $-300^\circ$ to radians (exact form).
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

The sign carries through: $-300 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = -\frac{5\pi}{3}$.

Tip: sanity check: it is **coterminal** with $\frac{\pi}{3}$, since $-\frac{5\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{\pi}{3}$.
Watch out: do not drop the minus sign; the angle is clockwise.

cards.title: What is $1^\circ$ in radians, exactly?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745$

It is the conversion factor itself: $180^\circ = \pi\text{ rad}$, so divide both sides by $180$.

Multiplying a degree measure by $\frac{\pi}{180}$ converts it to **radians**.
Tip: $\frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745$, so a degree is a very small angle.

cards.title: Convert $\frac{7\pi}{12}$ radians to degrees.
cards.body:
$105^\circ$

Replace $\pi$ with $180^\circ$: $\frac{7 \cdot 180^\circ}{12} = 7 \cdot 15^\circ = 105^\circ$.

Tip: each $\frac{\pi}{12}$ is $15^\circ$, so count in steps of $15^\circ$.

cards.title: Convert $2.5$ radians to degrees, to the nearest tenth of a degree.
cards.body:
$143.2^\circ$

Multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$: $2.5 \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{450}{\pi} \approx 143.24$, which rounds to $143.2^\circ$.

Key idea: a **radian** measure needn't contain $\pi$; $2.5$ rad is just an arc $2.5$ radii long.
cards.searchQuery: convert 2.5 radians to degrees nearest tenth

cards.title: Why is radian measure considered dimensionless?
cards.body:
A radian measure is a ratio of two lengths: $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$, arc length over radius.

A radian measure is a **ratio of two lengths**: $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$, arc length over radius.

The length units cancel, which is why $s = r\theta$ gives the arc length in the radius's units with no conversion factor.

Key idea: "rad" is a label, not a physical unit.
cards.searchQuery: radian dimensionless ratio arc length over radius

cards.title: Why does calculus measure angles in radians rather than degrees?
cards.body:
Only in radians do $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ hold.

Only in **radians** do $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ hold.

In degrees a stray factor appears: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^\circ) = \frac{\pi}{180}\cos(x^\circ)$.

Why: radians make arc length and angle the same number on the unit circle, which keeps these formulas clean.
cards.searchQuery: why radians calculus derivative sin x limit sin x over x

cards.title: A calculator returns $\sin 30 \approx -0.988$. What went wrong?
cards.body:
It was in radian mode, so it computed the sine of $30$ radians, not $30^\circ$.

The calculator was in **radian mode**, so it computed the sine of $30$ radians, not $30^\circ$.

Degree mode gives $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$; so does entering $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}$ in radian mode.

Tip: a sine of an acute angle is never negative, so a negative answer is a red flag.

cards.title: Convert $25^\circ 15' 36''$ to decimal degrees.
cards.body:
$25.26^\circ$

One minute is $\frac{1}{60}$ of a degree and one second is $\frac{1}{3600}$ of a degree: $25 + \frac{15}{60} + \frac{36}{3600} = 25 + 0.25 + 0.01 = 25.26$.

Watch out: minutes and seconds are base $60$, not decimals, so $25^\circ 15'$ is not $25.15^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: degrees minutes seconds to decimal degrees 25 15 36

cards.title: What are the complement and the supplement of $\frac{\pi}{5}$, in radians?
cards.body:
Complement $\frac{3\pi}{10}$; supplement $\frac{4\pi}{5}$.

Complementary angles sum to $\frac{\pi}{2}$: $\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{5} = \frac{5\pi - 2\pi}{10} = \frac{3\pi}{10}$.

Supplementary angles sum to $\pi$: $\pi - \frac{\pi}{5} = \frac{4\pi}{5}$.

Mnemonic: **C** comes before **S** and $90^\circ$ before $180^\circ$.

cards.title: In which quadrant does the terminal side of $\theta = 4$ radians lie?
cards.body:
Quadrant III.

$\pi \approx 3.14 < 4 < \frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$, so the terminal side is in **QIII**.

Tip: memorize the benchmarks $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$, $\pi \approx 3.14$, $\frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$ and $2\pi \approx 6.28$.

cards.title: In which quadrant does the terminal side of $-\frac{5\pi}{4}$ lie?
cards.body:
Quadrant II.

Turning clockwise, $-\pi$ reaches the negative $x$-axis, and the extra $\frac{\pi}{4}$ carries it up into **QII**.

Tip: sanity check: $-\frac{5\pi}{4} + 2\pi = \frac{3\pi}{4}$, a QII angle.
Tip: add $2\pi$ to a negative angle to see where it really points.

cards.title: Exact length of the arc subtended by a $60^\circ$ central angle in a circle of radius $9$?
cards.body:
$3\pi \approx 9.42$

Convert first: $60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}$, so $s = r\theta = 9 \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = 3\pi$.

Tip: sanity check: as a fraction of the circumference, $\frac{60}{360} \cdot 2\pi \cdot 9 = 3\pi$.
Watch out: the formula $s = r\theta$ needs **radians**, not degrees.
cards.searchQuery: arc length 60 degree central angle radius 9

cards.title: An arc of length $15\,\text{cm}$ lies on a circle of radius $6\,\text{cm}$. What central angle does it subtend, in radians?
cards.body:
$2.5\text{ rad}$

$\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{15}{6} = 2.5$ rad. The centimeters cancel, leaving a pure number of **radians** (about $143^\circ$).

Tip: the answer is in radians automatically, with no $\pi$ needed.
cards.searchQuery: central angle from arc length and radius theta = s/r

cards.title: An arc of length $10\pi$ subtends a central angle of $\frac{5\pi}{6}$. What is the radius?
cards.body:
$12$

Rearrange $s = r\theta$: $r = \frac{s}{\theta} = \frac{10\pi}{5\pi/6} = 10\pi \cdot \frac{6}{5\pi} = 12$.

Watch out: this works only with $\theta$ in **radians**.
cards.searchQuery: radius from arc length and central angle

cards.title: Exact area of a sector with radius $6$ and central angle $120^\circ$?
cards.body:
$12\pi$

A $120^\circ$ sector is $\frac{1}{3}$ of the disk: $\frac{1}{3} \cdot \pi \cdot 6^2 = 12\pi$.

Check in **radians**: $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 36 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} = 12\pi$.
Tip: the fraction-of-a-circle method needs no conversion to radians.

cards.title: A sector has radius $10$ and arc length $8$. What is its area?
cards.body:
$40$

Substitute $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$ into $A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ to get $A = \frac{1}{2}rs = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10 \cdot 8 = 40$.

Mnemonic: it looks like a triangle's area, with the arc as the base and the radius as the height.
cards.searchQuery: sector area from arc length A = 1/2 r s

cards.title: A sector of radius $4$ has area $24$. What is its central angle, in radians?
cards.body:
$3\text{ rad}$

Solve $A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ for $\theta$: $\theta = \frac{2A}{r^2} = \frac{48}{16} = 3$ rad.

Tip: sanity check: that is about $172^\circ$, just under a half-turn.
Tip: any answer above $2\pi \approx 6.28$ would mean more than a full circle.
cards.searchQuery: sector central angle from area radius theta = 2A/r^2

cards.title: For uniform circular motion, define angular speed $\omega$ and linear speed $v$, and give the relation between them.
cards.body:
$\omega = \frac{\theta}{t}$ (angle swept per unit time) and $v = \frac{s}{t}$ (arc length per unit time), so $v = r\omega$.

$\omega = \frac{\theta}{t}$ is the angle swept per unit time and $v = \frac{s}{t}$ is the arc length per unit time. With $s = r\theta$ this gives $v = r\omega$.

Watch out: $\omega$ must be in **radians** per unit time; convert rpm or degrees per second first.
cards.searchQuery: angular speed linear speed v = r omega

cards.title: A wheel of radius $0.3\,\text{m}$ spins at $10\,\text{rad/s}$. How fast does a point on its rim move, in $\text{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$3\,\text{m/s}$

$v = r\omega = 0.3 \cdot 10 = 3\,\text{m/s}$.

Radians are dimensionless, so $\text{m} \cdot \text{rad/s}$ is just $\text{m/s}$.
Tip: units check: length times angle per time is length per time.
cards.searchQuery: linear speed of wheel rim v = r omega

cards.title: Convert $45$ revolutions per minute to radians per second (exact).
cards.body:
$\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\,\text{rad/s} \approx 4.71\,\text{rad/s}$

Each revolution is $2\pi$ rad and each minute is $60\,\text{s}$: $45 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{60} = \frac{90\pi}{60} = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ rad/s, about $4.71$ rad/s.

Tip: to convert rpm to rad/s, multiply by $\frac{\pi}{30}$.
cards.searchQuery: rpm to radians per second 45 rpm

cards.title: A wheel of radius $2\,\text{ft}$ turns at $30$ rpm. What is the exact linear speed of a point on its rim, in $\text{ft/min}$?
cards.body:
$120\pi\,\text{ft/min} \approx 377\,\text{ft/min}$

Convert to **radians** first: $\omega = 30 \cdot 2\pi = 60\pi\,\text{rad/min}$. Then $v = r\omega = 2 \cdot 60\pi = 120\pi\,\text{ft/min}$, about $377\,\text{ft/min}$.

Watch out: using $30$ rpm directly in $v = r\omega$ skips the $2\pi$ per revolution.
cards.searchQuery: linear speed from rpm wheel radius 2 ft

cards.title: On a rigid spinning disk, which is the same for every point: angular speed or linear speed?
cards.body:
Angular speed.

Every point sweeps the same angle in the same time, so $\omega$ is shared.

But $v = r\omega$ grows with distance from the center, so points on the rim move **fastest**.

Example: the center point has $v = 0$ while $\omega$ is unchanged.
cards.searchQuery: rigid rotating disk same angular speed all points

cards.title: Two cities on the same meridian differ in latitude by $1^\circ$. Using Earth's radius $3960\,\text{mi}$, how far apart are they, to the nearest mile?
cards.body:
$69\,\text{mi}$

The arc subtends $1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180}$ rad at Earth's center: $s = r\theta = 3960 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = 22\pi \approx 69.1$ mi.

Tip: one degree of latitude is about $69$ miles, a good number to remember.
cards.searchQuery: latitude one degree distance miles earth radius 3960

cards.title: On the unit circle, how does the arc length from $(1, 0)$ to the terminal point of $\theta$ compare with $\theta$ in radians?
cards.body:
They're equal (for $\theta \ge 0$).

With $r = 1$, $s = r\theta$ becomes $s = \theta$.

That is why any real number $t$ can serve as an angle: travel a distance $|t|$ around the unit circle, counterclockwise if $t > 0$ and clockwise if $t < 0$.

Key idea: on the unit circle, angle in radians and distance traveled are the **same number**.
cards.searchQuery: unit circle arc length equals angle radians

cards.title: Starting at $(1, 0)$, you travel an arc of length $3\pi$ counterclockwise around the unit circle. At what point do you stop?
cards.body:
$(-1, 0)$

On the unit circle arc length equals angle, so this is $\theta = 3\pi = 2\pi + \pi$: one full lap, then a half-turn more.

You end at $(\cos\pi, \sin\pi) = (-1, 0)$.
Tip: strip full laps of $2\pi$ first.
cards.searchQuery: wrap arc length 3pi around unit circle endpoint

cards.title: If the terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(x, y)$, what are $\csc\theta$, $\sec\theta$, and $\cot\theta$?
cards.body:
$\csc\theta = \frac{1}{y}$, $\sec\theta = \frac{1}{x}$, $\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}$.

Each is undefined where its denominator is $0$: cosecant and cotangent when $y = 0$ (multiples of $\pi$), secant when $x = 0$.

Mnemonic: **co**secant goes with **si**ne's $y$, and secant goes with cosine's $x$; each reciprocal has the "other" co-prefix.
cards.searchQuery: cosecant secant cotangent unit circle definition

cards.title: A point $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ lies on the terminal side of $\theta$, and $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$. What are $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, and $\tan\theta$?
cards.body:
$\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}$, $\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}$, $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$ (when $x \ne 0$).

Dividing by $r$ scales the point onto the unit circle at $\left(\frac{x}{r}, \frac{y}{r}\right)$, so any point on the ray works.

Watch out: $r$ is a distance, so it is always **positive**; the signs come from $x$ and $y$.
cards.searchQuery: trig functions point on terminal side r = sqrt(x^2+y^2)

cards.title: The terminal side of $\theta$ passes through $(-3, 4)$. Find $\cos\theta$.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{3}{5}$

$r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = 5$, so $\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{5}$.

Tip: sanity check: the point is in QII, where cosine is **negative**.
Tip: check that $\left(\frac{x}{r}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{r}\right)^2 = 1$.

cards.title: The terminal side of $\theta$ passes through $(5, -12)$. Find $\csc\theta$.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{13}{12}$

$r = \sqrt{5^2 + (-12)^2} = 13$, so $\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = -\frac{12}{13}$ and $\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{13}{12}$.

Watch out: $r$ is always **positive**; the sign comes from $y$.

cards.title: The terminal side of $\theta$ passes through $(-1, -\sqrt{3})$. Find $\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi)$, in radians.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$

$r = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2$, so $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) = \left(-\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$. That is **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$ in QIII, so $\theta = \pi + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3}$.

Watch out: $\tan^{-1}$ alone would give $\frac{\pi}{3}$, the wrong quadrant.

cards.title: The point $\left(-\frac{3}{5}, y\right)$ is on the unit circle in Quadrant III. Find $y$.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{4}{5}$

$x^2 + y^2 = 1$ gives $y^2 = 1 - \frac{9}{25} = \frac{16}{25}$, so $y = \pm\frac{4}{5}$.

In QIII both coordinates are **negative**, so $y = -\frac{4}{5}$.
Watch out: the equation gives the size; the quadrant gives the sign.
cards.searchQuery: unit circle missing coordinate x^2+y^2=1 quadrant III

cards.title: At what exact point does the terminal side of $\frac{7\pi}{4}$ meet the unit circle?
cards.body:
$\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$

$\frac{7\pi}{4} = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{4}$ is in QIV with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{4}$: $x$ is positive, $y$ is negative, and both have size $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.
Tip: in QIV the signs are $(+, -)$.

cards.title: The terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(a, b)$. Where does the terminal side of $\theta + \pi$ meet it?
cards.body:
$(-a, -b)$

Adding $\pi$ is a half-turn, which sends each point to the opposite end of a diameter.

So $\sin(\theta + \pi) = -\sin\theta$ and $\cos(\theta + \pi) = -\cos\theta$, while $\tan(\theta + \pi) = \frac{-b}{-a} = \tan\theta$.

Key idea: tangent repeats every $\pi$, sine and cosine every $2\pi$.
cards.searchQuery: unit circle point theta plus pi half turn

cards.title: The terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(a, b)$. Where does the terminal side of $\pi - \theta$ meet it?
cards.body:
$(-a, b)$

$\pi - \theta$ is the mirror image of $\theta$ across the $y$-axis.

So supplementary angles share a sine and have opposite cosines: $\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\theta$ and $\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta$.
Example: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ gives $\pi - \theta = \frac{5\pi}{6}$, and $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\frac{\pi}{6}$.
cards.searchQuery: unit circle point pi minus theta reflection

cards.title: $\tan\theta$ equals what geometric property of the terminal side of $\theta$?
cards.body:
Its slope.

The terminal side runs from the origin through $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, so its slope is $\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$.

Example: the line $y = x$ makes a $45^\circ$ angle, and $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.
Tip: a vertical line has no slope, matching $\tan\frac{\pi}{2}$ being undefined.
cards.searchQuery: tangent as slope of terminal side unit circle

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\frac{\pi}{4}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

The $45^\circ$ point has equal coordinates, and $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ forces $2x^2 = 1$, so $x = y = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

Tip: $\sin\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{4}$ are equal.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cos\frac{\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

The $30^\circ$ point is $\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$, and cosine is the $x$-coordinate.

Tip: a small angle's point sits far to the right, so its cosine is the larger coordinate.
Watch out: do not swap with $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan 45^\circ$?
cards.body:
$1$

At $45^\circ$ the two coordinates are equal, so $\tan 45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 1$.

Tip: tangent is $\pm 1$ at every odd multiple of $45^\circ$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}$?
cards.body:
$-1$

$\frac{3\pi}{2}$ points straight down, to $(0, -1)$, and sine is the $y$-coordinate.

Its cosine is $0$, so $\tan\frac{3\pi}{2}$ is undefined.
Tip: the four axis points are $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(-1,0)$, $(0,-1)$ at $0$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cot\frac{\pi}{2}$?
cards.body:
$0$

$\cot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\cos(\pi/2)}{\sin(\pi/2)} = \frac{0}{1} = 0$.

Watch out: $\tan\frac{\pi}{2}$ is undefined, but cotangent at the same angle is simply $0$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sec\pi$?
cards.body:
$-1$

$\pi$ lands at $(-1, 0)$, so $\cos\pi = -1$ and $\sec\pi = \frac{1}{-1} = -1$.

Tip: secant equals $\pm 1$ exactly where cosine does, at the multiples of $\pi$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

$\frac{3\pi}{4} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{4}$ is in QII with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{4}$, and cosine is negative in QII.

So $\cos\frac{3\pi}{4} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.
Watch out: $\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}$ is not $+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$; the $x$-coordinate is left of the $y$-axis.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{2}$

$\frac{5\pi}{6} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$ is in QII with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$. Sine is positive in QII, so $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Tip: in QII sine keeps its sign and cosine flips.

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan\frac{2\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$-\sqrt{3}$

The point is $\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$, so $\tan\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{-1/2} = -\sqrt{3}$.

Tip: the **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$ gives the size; QII makes tangent negative.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sec\frac{2\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$-2$

$\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}$ (QII, **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$), and secant is its reciprocal: $\frac{1}{-1/2} = -2$.
Tip: find cosine first, then flip the fraction.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\frac{4\pi}{3} = \pi + \frac{\pi}{3}$ is in QIII with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$, and sine is negative in QIII.

So $\sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Watch out: do not confuse it with $\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = +\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, which is in QII.

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan\frac{5\pi}{4}$?
cards.body:
$1$

At $\frac{5\pi}{4}$ the point is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$, and two **negative**s make a positive ratio.

Tip: tangent is positive in QIII.

cards.title: Exact value of $\csc\frac{7\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$-2$

$\sin\frac{7\pi}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}$ (QIII, **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$), so $\csc\frac{7\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{-1/2} = -2$.
Tip: find sine first, then take the reciprocal.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cos\frac{5\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{2}$

$\frac{5\pi}{3} = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$ is in QIV with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Cosine is positive in QIV, so $\cos\frac{5\pi}{3} = \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Tip: in QIV cosine is positive and sine is negative.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sec\frac{11\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$

$\cos\frac{11\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (QIV, **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$), so $\sec\frac{11\pi}{6} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ after rationalizing.
Watch out: $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ are equal; the second is the rationalized form.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cot\frac{5\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$

The point is $\left(\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$, so $\cot\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{1/2}{-\sqrt{3}/2} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.
Tip: $\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}$, the **reciprocal** of the slope.

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan 240^\circ$?
cards.body:
$\sqrt{3}$

$240^\circ = 180^\circ + 60^\circ$ is in QIII, where tangent is **positive**, so $\tan 240^\circ = \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$.

Tip: tangent has period $180^\circ$, so $\tan(\theta + 180^\circ) = \tan\theta$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sec 225^\circ$?
cards.body:
$-\sqrt{2}$

$\cos 225^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ (QIII, **reference angle** $45^\circ$), so $\sec 225^\circ = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = -\sqrt{2}$.
Tip: $\sec\theta$ is $\frac{1}{\cos\theta}$, so a negative cosine gives a negative secant.

cards.title: Exact value of $\csc 300^\circ$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$

$\sin 300^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (QIV, **reference angle** $60^\circ$), so $\csc 300^\circ = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$.
Tip: $\csc\theta$ is $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$, so it has the same sign as sine.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\left(-\frac{7\pi}{4}\right)$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

Add $2\pi$: $-\frac{7\pi}{4} + 2\pi = \frac{\pi}{4}$, so the angle ends in QI and its sine is positive.

Watch out: a **negative** angle does not make the sine negative; only the terminal side matters.

cards.title: Exact value of $\tan\left(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$

$-\frac{5\pi}{6} + 2\pi = \frac{7\pi}{6}$, in QIII, where tangent is positive; the **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$ gives the size.

Check with oddness: $\tan\left(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\tan\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)$.
Tip: tangent is odd, so $\tan(-x) = -\tan x$.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cos\frac{13\pi}{6}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\frac{13\pi}{6} = 2\pi + \frac{\pi}{6}$, so it is **coterminal** with $\frac{\pi}{6}$ and has the same cosine.

Tip: strip off full turns of $2\pi = \frac{12\pi}{6}$ first.

cards.title: Exact value of $\sin\frac{11\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\frac{11\pi}{3} - 2\pi = \frac{5\pi}{3}$, which is in QIV with **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Sine is negative in QIV, so $\sin\frac{11\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Tip: subtract $2\pi = \frac{6\pi}{3}$ to reduce the angle.

cards.title: Exact value of $\cos 480^\circ$?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{1}{2}$

$480^\circ - 360^\circ = 120^\circ$, in QII with **reference angle** $60^\circ$. Cosine is negative there: $-\cos 60^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}$.
Tip: $480^\circ$ is one full turn plus $120^\circ$.

cards.title: If $\sin\theta < 0$ and $\tan\theta > 0$, in which quadrant does $\theta$ lie?
cards.body:
Quadrant III.

Sine is negative in QIII and QIV; tangent is positive in QI and QIII. Only **QIII** has both.

Why: there $x$ and $y$ are both negative, so $\frac{y}{x} > 0$.

cards.title: If $\cos\theta < 0$ and $\csc\theta > 0$, in which quadrant does $\theta$ lie?
cards.body:
Quadrant II.

$\csc\theta > 0$ means $\sin\theta > 0$ (QI or QII), and cosine is negative in QII and QIII. The overlap is **QII**.

Tip: convert each reciprocal function to its partner first.

cards.title: If $\sec\theta > 0$ and $\cot\theta < 0$, in which quadrant does $\theta$ lie?
cards.body:
Quadrant IV.

$\sec\theta > 0$ means $\cos\theta > 0$ (QI or QIV), and $\cot\theta$ has the sign of $\tan\theta$, which is negative in QII and QIV. The overlap is **QIV**.
Tip: sketch the signs of $x$ and $y$ in each quadrant.

cards.title: In which two quadrants is $\cos\theta$ negative?
cards.body:
Quadrants II and III.

Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, which is negative to the left of the $y$-axis. Secant, its **reciprocal**, has the same signs.
Tip: sine is negative in QIII and QIV, the lower half.

cards.title: Is $\sin 5$ positive or negative, with $5$ in radians?
cards.body:
Negative.

$\frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71 < 5 < 2\pi \approx 6.28$, so $5$ rad ends in QIV, where $y$-coordinates are negative. In fact $\sin 5 \approx -0.96$.

Watch out: here $5$ is in **radians**, not degrees; $\sin 5^\circ$ is positive.

cards.title: Is $\cos 2$ positive or negative, with $2$ in radians?
cards.body:
Negative.

$\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57 < 2 < \pi \approx 3.14$, so $2$ rad ends in QII, where $x$-coordinates are negative. In fact $\cos 2 \approx -0.42$.

Watch out: $2$ means **radians**; $\cos 2^\circ$ is positive.

cards.title: A student writes $\cos 210^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ because its reference angle is $30^\circ$. What is the correct exact value?
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

The reference angle gives only the **size**. $210^\circ$ is in QIII, where cosine is negative, so $\cos 210^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Tip: attach the quadrant's sign as a separate step.
cards.searchQuery: cos 210 degrees reference angle sign mistake

cards.title: How do you write every angle coterminal with $\theta$, in degrees and in radians?
cards.body:
$\theta + 360^\circ k$ or $\theta + 2\pi k$, for any integer $k$.

Coterminal angles share a terminal side, so all six trig functions agree on them.

Positive $k$ adds full counterclockwise turns; **negative** $k$ removes them.

Key idea: trig functions have period $2\pi$, so adding $2\pi k$ never changes their values.

cards.title: Find the angle in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ that is coterminal with $1000^\circ$.
cards.body:
$280^\circ$

Subtract whole turns: $1000^\circ - 2 \cdot 360^\circ = 280^\circ$.

Tip: estimate first. $\frac{1000}{360} \approx 2.8$, so two full turns come off.

cards.title: Find the angle in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ that is coterminal with $-250^\circ$.
cards.body:
$110^\circ$

Add one full turn: $-250^\circ + 360^\circ = 110^\circ$, a QII angle.

Tip: for a **negative** angle, keep adding $360^\circ$ until the result lands in range.

cards.title: Find the angle in $[0, 2\pi)$ that is coterminal with $\frac{23\pi}{4}$. Answer in radians.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$

In quarters, $2\pi = \frac{8\pi}{4}$, so remove two full turns: $\frac{23\pi}{4} - \frac{16\pi}{4} = \frac{7\pi}{4}$.

Tip: work in the fraction's own denominator to avoid slips.

cards.title: What is the reference angle of $300^\circ$, in degrees?
cards.body:
$60^\circ$

$300^\circ$ is in QIV, so the **reference angle** is $360^\circ - 300^\circ = 60^\circ$.

That is why $\cos 300^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin 300^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Tip: in QIV subtract from $360^\circ$.

cards.title: What is the reference angle of $-135^\circ$, in degrees?
cards.body:
$45^\circ$

$-135^\circ$ is coterminal with $225^\circ$ (QIII), and $225^\circ - 180^\circ = 45^\circ$.

Watch out: a **reference angle** is always positive and at most $90^\circ$, even for a negative angle.

cards.title: What is the reference angle of $\frac{11\pi}{4}$, in radians?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

First find the coterminal angle: $\frac{11\pi}{4} - 2\pi = \frac{3\pi}{4}$, in QII. Then $\pi - \frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
Tip: reduce to $[0, 2\pi)$ before finding the **reference angle**.

cards.title: What is the reference angle of $\theta = 2$ radians? Give an exact answer in radians.
cards.body:
$\pi - 2 \approx 1.14$

$2$ rad lies between $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$ and $\pi \approx 3.14$, so it is in QII, where the **reference angle** is $\pi - \theta$.

Key idea: reference angles needn't be nice fractions of $\pi$.

cards.title: Is a reference angle measured to the $x$-axis or to the $y$-axis?
cards.body:
The $x$-axis, always.

Example: $120^\circ$ has **reference angle** $60^\circ$ (to the negative $x$-axis), not $30^\circ$ (to the $y$-axis).

Watch out: measuring to the $y$-axis swaps the sine and cosine values.

cards.title: Which reference angle do $\frac{5\pi}{6}$, $\frac{7\pi}{6}$, and $\frac{11\pi}{6}$ share? Answer in radians.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

They are $\pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$, $\pi + \frac{\pi}{6}$ and $2\pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$.

Tip: in lowest terms, a denominator of $6$ means **reference angle** $\frac{\pi}{6}$, $4$ means $\frac{\pi}{4}$, and $3$ means $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

cards.title: Evaluate exactly: $\sin^2\frac{\pi}{4} + \cos\frac{\pi}{3}$.
cards.body:
$1$

$\sin^2\frac{\pi}{4} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$, so the sum is $1$.

Watch out: $\sin^2 x$ means $(\sin x)^2$, not $\sin(x^2)$.
cards.searchQuery: evaluate sin^2 pi/4 plus cos pi/3 exact

cards.title: Evaluate exactly: $2\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\cos\frac{\pi}{6}$.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

It equals $\sin\frac{\pi}{3}$, an instance of the double-angle formula $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$.
Tip: check by evaluating $\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: evaluate 2 sin cos pi/6 exact double angle

cards.title: Exact value of $\csc\pi$?
cards.body:
Undefined.

$\csc\pi = \frac{1}{\sin\pi} = \frac{1}{0}$.

Cosecant and cotangent are undefined at every multiple of $\pi$, where the unit-circle point has $y = 0$.
Watch out: undefined is not the same as $0$.
cards.searchQuery: csc pi undefined cosecant multiples of pi

cards.title: Which is larger, $\sin 1$ or $\cos 1$, with $1$ in radians?
cards.body:
$\sin 1$

$1\text{ rad} \approx 57.3^\circ$, and between $45^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ a unit-circle point's $y$-coordinate exceeds its $x$-coordinate.

Indeed $\sin 1 \approx 0.841$ and $\cos 1 \approx 0.540$.
Tip: sine and cosine cross at $\frac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785$; past that, sine is larger.
